1.pericope_label: That ye be not soon shaken in mind, as that the day of Christ is at hand

schools.summary: Barnes denies the opening is an adjuration at all, since Scripture does not adjure in view of an event, and gives three reasons for thinking a letter had been forged in the apostles' name; he illustrates the alarm from a year in which seventeen people were committed to one asylum expecting the Lord's appearing. Ellicott reads the preposition as the stronger for the sake of, distinguishes the tenses of shaken and troubled, and would insert a so before soon, since the readers had been shaken already in an unconscionably short time. Robertson notes the rare noun for the gathering, found in the Maccabees and on a stone at Syme, and takes it of the rapture.

Gill keeps to a misunderstanding of the earlier letter; Calvin treats the words as an earnest entreaty, since it is customary to adjure by what we revere, and looks behind the error to its use, that Satan, unable to overturn the hope of a resurrection openly, undermined it by promising a near day, as in the dreams of Lactantius and the old Chiliasts.

Clarke joins both senses of the disputed clause, the former letter misconceived and any other letter pretending to be from the apostles, and raises the question that governs the rest of the chapter, whether the coming meant is the judgment on the Jewish polity or the end of the world, answering that the prophecy has both in view.

Henry reads the opening as an oath and an appeal to what the readers themselves hope for, gathers all the saints of both testaments into the promised meeting, and allows that some may have pretended a private revelation.

debates.question: Is the opening phrase a solemn adjuration?

positions.view: yes, an oath by what the readers hope for
yes, and stronger than the simple by: for the sake of
no; it means simply concerning his coming

outliers.claim: in a single year seventeen people were admitted to one asylum whose minds had given way under the expectation that the Lord was about to appear

themes: Now we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by our gathering together unto him,
That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand.

3.pericope_label: Except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition

schools.summary: Barnes surveys and rejects the escapes offered for the missing antecedent, adopts Erasmus's judgment that the article marks the great and before-predicted apostasy, and argues from Daniel and the Apocalypse that a succession rather than a single man is meant; Ellicott says the article changes the purpose of the sentence from new prophecy to reminder, insists the apostates must once have held the faith since men cannot fall from ground they never occupied, and reads the figure as a rival Christ rather than a mere opponent; Robertson widens the warning past conversation and letter to tricks of any kind.

Clarke defines the word as a dereliction of the essential principles of religious truth and concedes that what the apostasy means has not yet, and perhaps never will be, answered to general satisfaction; his survey of the identifications runs from Caligula and Simon Magus to Mohammed, Napoleon and the papacy, and he reports Calmet's protest against the want of candour in Protestant writers.

Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the mechanism rather than the identification: hatred of the brethren makes room for Antichrist, since the devil prepares the divisions beforehand so that he who is to come may be acceptable.

debates.question: Does the man of sin mean one man or a succession?

positions.view: a succession, as king and beast stand for lines and empires in the prophets
probably an actual individual impersonating the movement

outliers.claim: he reports Calmet asking whether Protestant writers would be willing that Catholics should credit all the aspersions cast on Protestantism

themes: Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition;

4.pericope_label: Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, so that he sitteth in the temple of God

schools.summary: Barnes reads the temple as the Christian church as a society and applies the description to the papacy in detail, listing its claims over priesthood, kings and conscience and quoting the titles given the pope by Catholic writers without rebuke; Ellicott presses the word for temple to mean the sacred house itself, probably the Mercy Seat, yet denies a literal session was expected, and concludes that the great apostasy will not be atheistic but internal to the church; Robertson brings in Caligula's attempt to set his statue in the temple at Jerusalem.

Calvin uses the epithets structurally, since they set this kingdom in direct opposition to Christ's, which being spiritual makes the rival tyranny a tyranny over souls; he lists what Scripture reserves to God and finds the pope claiming every item of it, and raises a further variant turning on a single mistaken letter.
Clarke reports the words as God wanting in the chief uncials and most versions, quotes an editor that they should most certainly be erased, and thinks the text reads better without them.

debates.question: Are the words as God part of the text?

positions.view: doubtful, but the sense is not materially affected

outliers.claim: the great apostasy will most probably not become avowedly atheistic but will be an apostasy within the church, its head claiming the honours she pays to the living God

themes: Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.

5.pericope_label: Now ye know what withholdeth: for the mystery of iniquity doth already work

schools.summary: Barnes says much of the obscurity comes from an allusion to teaching now lost, argues the restraint must be outside the church and so takes it of civil power, reports that the primitive Christians prayed for the peace of the empire knowing the man of sin would rise on its ruins, and treats the word mystery as hidden rather than unintelligible; Ellicott notes the imperfect tense and the singular pronoun and suggests the writer may shrink from naming the withholder for fear the power should discover his prophecies; Robertson says plainly that we do not know what is meant.
Calvin notes the mildness of the reproof, that it is fatherly to say only that they had let forgetfulness steal in upon a matter so useful.
Clarke observes that the writer speaks with great caution and does not wish to publish in writing what he had said in private, the hints dropped being enough to recall the whole.

Henry gives the identification in a sentence, that the power supposed is the Roman empire, not named more plainly at the time, and holds that corruption of doctrine and worship came in by degrees while the apostles were still living.

Chrysostom states the alternatives and decides for the Roman empire against the grace of the Spirit, on the grounds that the Spirit would have been named plainly and that the gifts have long since ceased; and he explains the obscurity as prudence, since to say openly that the empire would be dissolved would have got the writer overwhelmed as a pestilent person and all the faithful with him.

debates.question: What is it that withholds the man of sin?

positions.view: the Roman empire, named obscurely for prudence
some present and tangible power the writer will not name in writing
unknown; the clue is lost with the oral teaching

outliers.claim: the obscurity is deliberate: naming the Roman empire would have brought superfluous enmities and useless dangers on the writer and on all the faithful

themes: Remember ye not, that, when I was yet with you, I told you these things?
And now ye know what withholdeth that he might be revealed in his time.
For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way.

8.pericope_label: Whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth: whose coming is after the working of Satan

schools.summary: Barnes offers two readings of the breath of the mouth, the word spoken at the coming or the truth already spoken, granting that the most obvious interpretation refers both clauses to the same period, and insists the word rendered brightness means merely an appearing with no necessary idea of splendour; Ellicott restores the title the Lawless One, finds the point of the borrowed phrase in the perfect ease of the destruction, and says that when the true and the false Christ stand face to face there will be no possibility of delusion any more; Robertson calls the whole a grand fiasco and notes that the rival has his own presence and epiphany.

Calvin argues from contraries, that a power standing only by Satan's impostures must vanish as soon as Christ shines forth, since it reigns only in darkness; and holds Satan so limited that he cannot injure the elect at all, which he offers as a necessary consolation.

Clarke will have only the gradual sense, since it is by the preaching of the truth that this power is exposed, so its death will not be sudden; and he keeps the distinction that these miracles are only appearances of what was real, while God sent real ones such as Satan cannot produce.

positions.view: the truth was offered and refused; the phrase implies nothing about predestination
the elect cannot be injured, this power having no strength except by God's permission

outliers.claim: to be too indolent to examine whether a thing be true is already to reject the love of the truth, which is worse than not accepting the truth itself

themes: And then shall that Wicked be revealed, whom the Lord shall consume with the spirit of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming:
Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders,
And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved.

11.pericope_label: God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie

schools.summary: Barnes admits the divine agency is distinctly recognised but argues that no positive influence need be supposed, since the force of the language is met by God withdrawing all restraint; he denies that the particle in the following verse must carry purpose, since it may mark result only, and holds it cannot be proved that God sends delusions in order that men may be damned. Ellicott describes the mechanism, that God takes away by his natural law the power of discerning true from false, cites Ahab and the lying spirit, corrects the tense and the rendering, and reads the following particle as purpose outright; Robertson calls it the definite judicial act of God.

Gill will not have it a bare permission but a voluntary one, distinguishing the efficacy of error as a punishment for sin rather than a sin of which God could be the author; Calvin is the most positive, holding that God delivers over to a reprobate mind those he has appointed to destruction, and points to a specimen he takes to be already visible.

Clarke keeps the milder verb throughout, that God permits the delusion to occupy their minds, so that they are ever ready to receive any false Christ while rejecting the true, and makes their condemnation the effect of a refusal to believe grounded in love of their sins.

debates.question: Does the particle in verse twelve express purpose or result?

positions.view: purpose: this is God's design in making them believe the lie
result only; it cannot be proved that God sends delusion in order that men be damned

outliers.claim: a terrible combination when God and Satan are agreed to deceive a man, and yet an encouragement to see God using Satan for his own purposes

themes: And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie:
That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness.

13.pericope_label: God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation: stand fast, and hold the traditions

schools.summary: Barnes draws four propositions from the one clause, that election, eternal election and personal election are all true and all proper grounds of thanksgiving, guarding it by the rule that no one has evidence of being chosen except as he has evidence of being sanctified; and he gives five reasons why the verse furnishes no authority for later traditions. Ellicott presses the tenses of beloved and chose, and argues that the exhortation to stand fast is in itself conclusive against irreversible predestination, while quoting Chrysostom with approval that the tradition of the church is worthy of belief without further question.

Clarke sets the order of grace out as six stages and argues from the sequence that the calling did not necessarily and irresistibly lead to faith, nor faith to sanctification, nor sanctification to glory, since a man might halt at any stage; he denies the verse can support traditions taken from neither Testament and spoken by neither prophet nor apostle.

Henry finds the consolation in the remnant according to the election of grace, joins the end and the means so that we are not chosen because we were holy but that we might be holy, and refuses to let the doctrine excuse carelessness, since grace in election is so far from superseding our care that it should quicken us to the greatest resolution; on the traditions he allows the verse its force for its own time, the canon not yet being complete, and denies any argument from it now.

debates.question: Does the exhortation to stand fast tell against irreversible predestination?

positions.view: yes; it would be needless if they could not quit their ground
the doctrine stands, but should quicken diligence rather than excuse it
election, eternal and personal, is simply true and a ground of praise

outliers.claim: he quotes Chrysostom with approval that not all tradition was delivered by letter and that both kinds are equally worthy of belief: it is tradition, ask no further questions

themes: But we are bound to give thanks alway to God for you, brethren beloved of the Lord, because God hath from the beginning chosen you to salvation through sanctification of the Spirit and belief of the truth:
Whereunto he called you by our gospel, to the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.

16.pericope_label: Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father, comfort your hearts

schools.summary: Barnes calls the prayer one really offered to the Saviour, language possible only to one who thought him divine, and turns the conjunction back on those who would use it to separate the Persons; he contrasts the joys of religion with every other kind, which fade and terminate at death; and he closes the chapter defending the apostles against the charge of having expected an imminent end. Ellicott denies the unusual order of names was designed to prove equality and suggests a climax instead, and joins hope to grace so closely that the prospect belongs to us only in grace; Robertson notes the singular participle and the remark that these letters never use a plural verb of two Persons together.
Calvin takes the ascription of a divine work as clear proof of Christ's divinity and infers that we obtain nothing from God unless we seek it in him.

Clarke sets the gospel's threefold testimony, believe, love, obey, against the maxim that believing the doctrines makes a man safe, since the faith of a devil may exist without loving obedience; and he closes by refusing to fix any specific meaning to the apostasy, the man of sin or the restrainer, having found it too difficult to satisfy himself.

Henry makes comfort and establishment reciprocal, since pleasure in the ways of God helps us persevere and steadiness is what makes the joys of religion possible, and asks what lies at the bottom of all our uneasiness but our unsteadiness; he grounds the hope on the love and promise of God and on experience, not on merit.

debates.question: What does the prayer being addressed to Christ prove?

positions.view: his divinity, since such language is possible only of a divine person
nothing by design; equality is established only incidentally, the order forming a climax

outliers.claim: having gone through the chapter word by word he declines to fix any meaning at all, since the variety of explanations by wise and learned men only proves the difficulty of the place

themes: Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father, which hath loved us, and hath given us everlasting consolation and good hope through grace,
Comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work.
